newsitem.title: UK: Reed, Burmah up on expected FIDs move.
newsitem.headline: Reed, Burmah up on expected FIDs move.

text.p: Expectations that the UK government could reverse its proposed abolition of foreign income dividends (FIDs) as early as Thursday afternoon lifted shares in companies with a high proportion of foreign earnings, analysts and traders said.

At 1011 GMT, publisher Reed had gained 3-1/2p to 586-1/2p, lubricants group Burmah traded 15-1/2p higher at 982, mining group Rio Tinto Plc had risen 7p to 1,014-1/2p and GKN Plc was up 10-1/2p at 948-1/2p.
"A lot of these companies were hit very badly when the budget came through so this would neutralise what would happen when the abolition was proposed," one analyst said.
Billiton, the South African mining house that plans to become a UK-listed company later this month, may also benefit from the reversal, analysts said.
The Financial Times said Britain would not abolish FIDs in April 1999 as Chancellor (finance minister) Gordon Brown outlined in the new Labour administration's first budget last week.
Retaining FIDs would allow companies to continue to enjoy tax advantages. FIDs were introduced in 1993 to prevent the double taxation of dividends.
But shares in some companies that warned against the abolition of FIDs did not join in the rally.
Oil exploration group LASMO Plc fell 10-1/2p to 263-1/2p.
Shawn Reynolds, an energy analyst at Lehman Brothers, said abolition of FIDs would not have had a substantive impact on Lasmo's bottom line.
"If it was actually abolished, Lasmo would have been hurt by it, but only marginally," he said. "I don't think it means that much for Lasmo."
